sections.text: For Graves disease in the first three months of pregnancy, NIDDK describes propylthiouracil as commonly used because methimazole can rarely harm the fetus. Radioiodine is not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Radioiodine destroys hormone-producing thyroid cells, and hypothyroidism often develops afterward. These principles do not establish patient-specific dosing.

question.stem: After radioiodine for hyperthyroidism, a patient develops thyroid hormone deficiency. Which explanation best fits the treatment mechanism?

choices.text: A temporary symptom-masking effect without loss of hormone-producing cells
The later deficiency establishes that the original hyperthyroidism diagnosis was wrong
Radioiodine destroys hormone-producing cells, so subsequent hypothyroidism is an anticipated consequence
Radioiodine reduces heart rate without affecting hormone-producing thyroid cells
The deficiency should be dismissed without thyroid follow-up because treatment was completed

question.explanation: NIDDK explains that radioiodine destroys hormone-producing thyroid cells and that hypothyroidism commonly follows treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: NIDDK describes destruction of thyroid hormone-producing cells rather than symptom masking alone.
distractorExplanations.B: The source describes later hypothyroidism as a possible consequence of radioiodine treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: The source describes direct destruction of thyroid cells, not only heart-rate reduction.
distractorExplanations.E: The reference describes subsequent thyroid deficiency requiring management, so completed treatment does not dismiss the finding.

question.learningObjective: Explain thyroid hormone deficiency after radioiodine treatment.

question.stem: An adult has a newly detected thyroid nodule and subnormal TSH. Which additional test best evaluates whether the nodule is functioning?

choices.text: A radionuclide thyroid scan
Routine thyroglobulin as the sole test
A fasting lipid panel
A D-dimer
No evaluation because all nodules are malignant

distractorExplanations.C: It does not evaluate thyroid function.

question.stem: A euthyroid adult has a 1.4-cm solid hypoechoic thyroid nodule with microcalcifications. Which next diagnostic action best follows the ATA high-suspicion pathway?

choices.text: Ignore it because TSH is normal
Perform ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration
Repeat imaging only after ten years
Treat immediately with insulin
Use a normal TSH as proof of benign histology

question.explanation: A high-suspicion nodule ≥1 cm meets the ATA FNA criterion.

distractorExplanations.A: Normal TSH does not establish benign histology.
distractorExplanations.C: That fails the indicated evaluation.
distractorExplanations.D: Insulin does not evaluate a thyroid nodule.
distractorExplanations.E: TSH does not establish histology.

question.stem: A euthyroid adult has a newly palpable thyroid nodule without prior imaging. Which investigation directly characterizes the nodule and helps assess malignancy likelihood?

choices.text: Thyroid antibody testing to define the nodule’s structure
Thyroid ultrasound
A TSH measurement as a complete structural characterization
Radioactive iodine uptake alone to characterize all structural features
Classify the nodule solely from the normal thyroid hormone result

question.explanation: NIDDK describes ultrasound as commonly used to examine thyroid nodules and assess whether they are more likely cancerous.

distractorExplanations.A: Antibodies help assess autoimmune disease; they do not provide the structural nodule image requested.
distractorExplanations.C: TSH assesses thyroid function rather than the ultrasound features of the nodule.
distractorExplanations.D: Uptake assesses thyroid iodine handling; the reference identifies ultrasound for closer structural examination of nodules.
distractorExplanations.E: Normal hormone function does not supply the nodule characterization requested.

question.learningObjective: Select structural assessment for a newly detected thyroid nodule.

question.stem: An adult with BMI 34 wants a structured initial weight-management plan. Which program best reflects comprehensive lifestyle intervention?

choices.text: Diet advice alone with no follow-up
Only a promise of rapid weight loss
Behavioral support, dietary changes and physical activity
Avoiding all activity indefinitely
A supplement without assessment

question.explanation: Comprehensive intervention combines behavioral, dietary and physical-activity components.

distractorExplanations.A: It omits two core components.
distractorExplanations.B: A promise does not constitute a program.
distractorExplanations.D: It omits physical activity.
distractorExplanations.E: It is not a comprehensive intervention.

question.learningObjective: Identify the components of a comprehensive obesity intervention.

sources.edition: September 2025

sections.title: Combine lifestyle components
sections.text: A comprehensive intervention combines behavioral support, dietary changes and physical activity. An energy deficit supports weight loss; no single dietary pattern is universally preferred.

question.stem: A nonpregnant adult has BMI 28 and hypertension. Lifestyle support continues, and no contraindications to weight-management medicines are identified. Which option is supported by the 2025 VA/DoD guideline?

choices.text: Medicines are always prohibited below BMI 40
Replace lifestyle support entirely with medication
Prescribe thyroid hormone despite normal thyroid function
Consider semaglutide or tirzepatide alongside lifestyle intervention
Wait until a cardiovascular event occurs

question.explanation: BMI ≥27 plus an obesity-associated condition meets the guideline category for these medications with lifestyle support.

distractorExplanations.A: That is not the guideline threshold.
distractorExplanations.B: The recommendation includes lifestyle intervention.
distractorExplanations.C: That is not the supported option here.
distractorExplanations.E: The recommendation does not require a prior event.

question.learningObjective: Apply the medication eligibility category without treating it as a patient-specific prescription.

question.stem: An adult weighing 200 pounds asks for a realistic example of an initial weight-loss goal. Which option corresponds to the NIDDK example rather than a guaranteed outcome?

choices.text: Ten pounds over six months, individualized with the clinician
Ten pounds as a mandatory target with no individualized time frame
Wait for a weight-related complication before discussing any target
Use the same pound target for every starting body weight
Treat reaching the example target as proof that all future disease risk is removed

question.explanation: NIDDK gives a possible initial goal of 5% over six months; 5% of 200 pounds is ten pounds. The goal remains individualized.

distractorExplanations.B: The reference presents a possible goal to tailor with the clinician, not a mandatory identical target.
distractorExplanations.C: The source recommends discussing an individualized goal rather than waiting for a complication.
distractorExplanations.D: The reference uses a proportion of starting weight, with individualization.
distractorExplanations.E: The reference describes possible health benefits, not guaranteed elimination of all future risk.

question.learningObjective: Apply a proportionate example of an individualized initial weight goal.

Track intake daily but omit activity and regular feedback
Monitor only during counseling appointments
Use one initial weigh-in as a replacement for subsequent monitoring
Daily intake/activity monitoring with weekly weight monitoring and feedback

Order it solely because of age
Replace all follow-up with imaging
Schedule urgent angiography despite no change
Avoid routine periodic testing without a clinical change

question.explanation: Unchanged clinical/functional status does not warrant routine periodic ischemic testing.

distractorExplanations.A: Automatic testing is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.B: Age alone is not the stated indication.

question.stem: A patient with chronic CAD has no MI in the past year, LVEF 60%, no angina and no other beta-blocker indication. Which statement best reflects the 2023 guideline?

choices.text: Routine long-term beta blocker is not recommended solely to improve outcomes in this scenario
All such patients require lifelong beta blockers solely for survival
Beta blockers replace statins
Exercise must be prohibited
Dietary supplements replace secondary-prevention medication

question.explanation: The guideline distinguishes antianginal or other indications from unsupported routine outcome-only beta-blocker use.

distractorExplanations.B: The guideline does not make that blanket recommendation.
distractorExplanations.C: They do not replace lipid treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Activity is part of chronic disease care.
distractorExplanations.E: Supplements do not replace recommended prevention.

sections.title: Treat angina and distinguish indications
sections.text: A beta blocker or calcium-channel blocker is first-line antianginal therapy. Long-term beta blockers are not recommended solely to improve outcomes without recent MI, LVEF ≤50% or another indication.

question.stem: A clinician has selected a stress test for a stable coronary disease study case, but the patient cannot exercise because of a mobility limitation. Which adaptation is described by NHLBI?

choices.text: Cancel the selected stress assessment solely because treadmill exercise is not feasible
Use only a resting ECG as if it creates the same cardiac stress
Use an appropriate medicine to make the heart work harder during the selected stress test
Use the mobility limitation to infer coronary artery status without the selected assessment
Require treadmill exercise despite the documented inability

question.explanation: NHLBI describes pharmacologic stress when a medical problem prevents exercise. This answers an already-selected test adaptation, not an indication to test everyone.

distractorExplanations.A: The reference describes medicine-based stress when a medical problem prevents exercise.
distractorExplanations.B: The question asks how to adapt the selected stress test; resting electrical assessment is not the described adaptation.
distractorExplanations.D: A limitation preventing exercise does not itself answer the diagnostic question.
distractorExplanations.E: The reference describes an alternative when exercise cannot be performed.

question.learningObjective: Adapt an indicated coronary stress test to inability to exercise.

question.stem: An adult completes PCI for ACS, has no high bleeding risk and no indication for chronic anticoagulation. What is the guideline default antiplatelet plan?

choices.text: No antiplatelet treatment after discharge
Aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor for at least 12 months
Aspirin only for two days in every case
An anticoagulant replaces both in every patient
Routine indefinite triple therapy for all

question.explanation: The default is at least 12 months of DAPT when high bleeding risk is absent.

distractorExplanations.C: That is not the default duration or combination.
distractorExplanations.D: No anticoagulation indication is supplied.

question.stem: A patient with acute MI develops cardiogenic shock and has a culprit artery plus additional nonculprit stenoses. Which strategy best follows the guideline?

choices.text: Delay revascularization until an outpatient appointment
Routine immediate PCI of every lesion regardless of culprit status
Emergency culprit-vessel revascularization without routine simultaneous nonculprit PCI
Treat only with dietary counseling
Use cardiac rehabilitation as the acute shock treatment

question.explanation: Emergency culprit revascularization is indicated; routine simultaneous nonculprit PCI is not.

distractorExplanations.E: Rehabilitation is a later prevention measure.

Attribute the new symptoms to diabetes without considering a coronary event
Exclude another attack because the symptoms differ from a prior episode
Consider a coronary event only if the pain becomes sudden and severe
A heart attack remains possible despite mild or atypical symptoms

question.learningObjective: Avoid excluding acute coronary events because typical severe pain is absent.

question.stem: A patient with known heart failure reports new weight gain, ankle swelling and increasing breathlessness. Which interpretation best fits NHLBI and guides reassessment?

choices.text: Attribute the findings to stable disease without reviewing the change from baseline
Possible worsening fluid buildup requiring clinical reassessment
Treat the findings only as an exercise-conditioning issue
Monitor the weight change without assessing the increasing breathlessness
Interpret ankle swelling in isolation and disregard the combined pattern

question.explanation: NHLBI identifies this combination as possible fluid buildup and recommends discussing monitoring and when to seek care.

distractorExplanations.A: NHLBI identifies these changes as possible fluid buildup requiring attention.
distractorExplanations.C: That assumption does not address the source’s warning about possible fluid buildup.
distractorExplanations.D: NHLBI includes increasing shortness of breath as a warning change alongside weight and swelling.
distractorExplanations.E: The reference identifies the combined changes as possible worsening fluid accumulation.

question.learningObjective: Recognize signs of worsening fluid accumulation in heart failure.

Stop all prescribed therapy before reviewing the new products

Review the complete medicine list with the clinician and pharmacist

question.stem: A patient has paroxysmal AF and validated annual stroke risk above 2%. Renal function permits a DOAC, there is no mechanical valve or significant mitral stenosis, and there is no other antiplatelet indication. Which strategy best follows the guideline?

Use an appropriate DOAC after shared decision-making
Prevent stroke only during symptomatic episodes
Use aspirin plus clopidogrel instead of anticoagulation
Ignore stroke risk if the office pulse is regular

question.explanation: Stroke prevention follows thromboembolic risk regardless of AF pattern; eligible patients generally favor a DOAC.

distractorExplanations.A: AF pattern does not eliminate the risk-based indication.
distractorExplanations.C: That is not the recommended risk-based strategy.
distractorExplanations.D: Dual antiplatelets are not the recommended substitute.

question.stem: After rate-control treatment for atrial fibrillation, a patient feels better but remains in AF. Which interpretation is accurate?

choices.text: Equate slower ventricular rate with documented restoration of normal rhythm
Infer that symptom improvement removes the separate clot-prevention question
Rate control can slow ventricular beating and improve symptoms while the abnormal rhythm continues
Require a normal rhythm before recognizing any benefit from rate control
Treat improvement in symptoms as the end of ongoing AF management

question.explanation: NHLBI explains that rate control allows ventricular filling and may improve symptoms while the abnormal rhythm continues.

distractorExplanations.A: NHLBI distinguishes rate control from rhythm restoration.
distractorExplanations.B: The reference treats clot prevention and rate/rhythm management as distinct aims.
distractorExplanations.D: The source describes improved symptoms while the abnormal rhythm continues.

All patients require catheter venography
DVT can be excluded without additional testing in this pathway

A negative result confirms PE

distractorExplanations.B: Confirmed proximal DVT needs treatment.

Classify permanent kidney failure immediately

A benzodiazepine

A thyroid suppressant without thyroid disease

Most suspected failures are reinfections, but when reinfection is unlikely and failure is suspected, obtain relevant specimens for culture, preferably with simultaneous NAAT, and susceptibility testing if gonorrhea is isolated before retreatment. Specialist/public-health consultation is part of this pathway.

question.stem: A patient has confirmed tinea corporis. A colleague proposes a topical antifungal combined with a high-potency corticosteroid. Which response reflects CDC stewardship guidance?

choices.text: Use the steroid combination because steroids eradicate dermatophytes
Choose an appropriate antifungal without a steroid whenever possible
Replace all antifungal treatment with prednisone
Assume a stronger steroid always shortens treatment
Treat only itch and ignore fungal persistence

question.explanation: Steroid-containing combinations can worsen fungal skin infection.

distractorExplanations.A: Steroids are not antifungal therapy.
distractorExplanations.C: Prednisone does not eradicate dermatophytes.
distractorExplanations.D: Steroids can prolong treatment problems.
distractorExplanations.E: Symptom relief is not eradication.

question.stem: A fictional adult has confirmed localized tinea corporis and no relevant drug contraindication. Symptoms improve after several days of an appropriate topical antifungal. Which instruction follows CDC's skin-ringworm guidance?

choices.text: Stop the antifungal once itch improves even if the directed course is unfinished
Switch to an oral antifungal solely because symptoms are improving
Replace the antifungal with a topical steroid as maintenance for residual redness
Apply the antifungal only on days with visible symptoms rather than follow instructions
Continue the topical antifungal for the product-directed duration even when symptoms improve

question.explanation: CDC advises using skin antifungal treatment for as long as directed, commonly 2–4 weeks depending on the product. Early symptom improvement is not the sole stopping rule.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC says to apply the antifungal for as long as directed, despite early improvement.
distractorExplanations.B: The described response does not replace the source's instruction to complete appropriate directed skin treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: This replaces the antifungal rather than completing the product-directed course described by CDC.
distractorExplanations.D: Intermittent symptom-triggered use does not implement the directed course in this vignette.

Seek reassessment and report severity, treatment response and travel history
Add a topical steroid to suppress the persistent rash

question.stem: In a fictional board vignette, a 34-year-old nonpregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired pneumonic plague. Relevant medication allergies and contraindications are absent. Which drug is in the CDC adult FIRST-LINE category for pneumonic plague? This question asks for the category, not a complete patient-specific regimen.

choices.text: Doxycycline
Levofloxacin
Azithromycin
Metronidazole
Vancomycin

question.explanation: CDC Table 1 places levofloxacin among first-line adult agents for pneumonic or septicemic plague. Doxycycline is an alternative for these forms. Severity still determines whether one agent or two distinct classes are appropriate.

distractorExplanations.A: Doxycycline is listed as an alternative for pneumonic or septicemic plague; its first-line designation for bubonic or pharyngeal disease does not answer this question.

sections.title: First-line antibiotics for adult pneumonic or septicemic plague
sections.text: In CDC Table 1, the first-line agents for adults aged at least 18 years with pneumonic or septicemic plague are ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin and streptomycin. These are multiple recommended options, not a single universally best drug. Route and selection depend on severity, ability to tolerate oral medication and individual factors. Pregnancy and neonatal recommendations require their separate source sections; this adult list does not establish their regimen.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Antimicrobial Treatment of Adults and Children; Table 1, Adults aged ≥18 years, First-line category; separate special-population recommendations.

sections.title: Doxycycline depends on the clinical form
sections.text: CDC classifies doxycycline as an alternative for pneumonic or septicemic plague, but as a first-line option for bubonic or pharyngeal plague. A stable patient with naturally acquired primary bubonic or pharyngeal disease and no secondary pneumonic or septicemic involvement can receive one recommended antimicrobial. Progression to pneumonic or septicemic disease changes which treatment recommendations apply. Do not transfer the bubonic first-line designation to pneumonic plague.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Pneumonic and Septicemic Plague, doxycycline discussion; Bubonic and Pharyngeal Plague, opening and final paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2.

sections.title: Severity changes the treatment strategy
sections.text: When the clinical and exposure history clearly indicates naturally occurring plague, CDC allows consideration of a single recommended agent for mild-to-moderate pneumonic or septicemic disease. Severe pneumonic or septicemic plague calls for two distinct antimicrobial classes initially, with narrowing to one agent after clinical improvement. This differs from treating every plague presentation with monotherapy regardless of severity.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Pneumonic and Septicemic Plague; paragraphs beginning 'If clinical and exposure history clearly indicate naturally occurring plague' and 'For patients with severe septicemic or pneumonic disease'.

question.stem: A fictional nonpregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired pneumonic plague with severe respiratory illness. There is no meningeal involvement and effective drugs from different classes are available. Which initial antimicrobial STRATEGY follows CDC guidance for severe pneumonic plague?

choices.text: Use no antibiotics until the illness becomes mild
Use a single agent in every case regardless of severity
Use the 7-day exposure-prophylaxis strategy instead of treatment
Start two distinct antimicrobial classes; narrow after clinical improvement
Select a bubonic-only recommendation without considering pulmonary disease

question.explanation: For severe pneumonic or septicemic plague, CDC recommends initial dual therapy using two distinct antimicrobial classes and narrowing to a single agent after clinical improvement. The mild-to-moderate naturally acquired monotherapy allowance does not fit this severe presentation.

distractorExplanations.A: The source calls for effective treatment of severe disease, not withholding it until severity changes.
distractorExplanations.B: The monotherapy consideration applies to clearly naturally occurring mild-to-moderate disease, not every severity.
distractorExplanations.C: This is symptomatic severe infection, not an exposure-only prophylaxis scenario.
distractorExplanations.E: Pulmonary disease belongs under the pneumonic/septicemic recommendations.

question.learningObjective: Apply the severe-pneumonic-plague dual-class strategy and its de-escalation condition.

question.stem: In a fictional exposure vignette, an asymptomatic adult had prolonged close contact within 6 feet of a coughing person with confirmed pneumonic plague and wore no adequate personal protective equipment. Which CDC prevention statement best fits this exposure?

choices.text: Consider postexposure antimicrobial prophylaxis for 7 days
No prophylaxis consideration is needed because the exposed adult has no symptoms
Use a severe-infection dual-class treatment strategy solely because exposure occurred
Treat every protected and unprotected contact identically
Use a single day of prophylaxis

question.explanation: Close, sustained contact with a pneumonic-plague patient without adequate protection is a CDC postexposure-prophylaxis consideration. CDC recommends 7 days for postexposure prophylaxis. This does not establish a symptomatic-infection treatment regimen.

distractorExplanations.B: Postexposure prevention concerns exposure risk and can apply before symptoms develop.
distractorExplanations.C: The severe-treatment strategy is for severe infection; this vignette describes an asymptomatic exposure.
distractorExplanations.D: CDC distinguishes inadequate protection from health care personnel who maintained standard and droplet precautions.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated CDC postexposure duration is 7 days, not one day.

question.learningObjective: Separate plague exposure prophylaxis from symptomatic treatment and retain protection criteria.

question.stem: A fictional nonpregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired tularemia without meningitis. Four first-line options are being reviewed under the CDC 2025 guideline. Which statement accurately describes the CURRENT recommendation categories?

choices.text: Streptomycin is the sole first-line treatment and every other drug is third-tier
Amoxicillin is first-line because all beta-lactams are effective against tularemia
Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and doxycycline are first-line options; streptomycin is third-tier
Doxycycline is never a treatment option in adults
All agents share one recommendation category with no patient-specific modifiers

question.explanation: The 2025 CDC recommendations list ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and doxycycline as first-line options for adults and children aged at least 1 month. Streptomycin is third-tier. Severity, delay, pregnancy and neuroinvasive involvement can change selection; first-line status is not a universal patient-specific prescription.

distractorExplanations.A: This repeats an older unqualified framing; streptomycin is third-tier in the 2025 update.
distractorExplanations.B: The guideline states that beta-lactams are ineffective for tularemia.
distractorExplanations.D: Doxycycline is included in the adult first-line list, although some scenarios favor other drugs.
distractorExplanations.E: The source separates first-line, alternative and third-tier categories and includes clinical modifiers.

question.learningObjective: Use the current CDC tularemia treatment ranking instead of an unsupported historical mnemonic.

sections.title: First-line treatment and age boundaries
sections.text: CDC's 2025 recommendations list ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and doxycycline as first-line treatment options for adults and children aged at least 1 month. Neonates aged 28 days or younger have a separate first-line list of ciprofloxacin or gentamicin. Selection depends on severity, availability, route and adverse-effect considerations. The adult list is not a blanket pregnancy or neonatal recommendation, and an age between these source-defined groups must not be assigned a regimen by extrapolation.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — Treatment recommendation for adults and children; Table 1 population categories; separate pregnancy and neonatal recommendations.

sections.title: Clinical forms and antibiotics that do not treat tularemia
sections.text: The guideline says ulceroglandular, pneumonic and typhoidal tularemia can be treated with the recommended ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin or doxycycline options; meningitis is a separate exception. Beta-lactams, including penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems, are ineffective for tularemia even when some laboratory susceptibility results appear favorable. Polymyxins, glycopeptides and sulfonamides are also ineffective. Do not substitute a routine beta-lactam regimen for source-supported tularemia treatment.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction — paragraph listing ineffective antimicrobial classes; Recommendations — Clinical Considerations for Treatment Recommendations, opening paragraph.

sections.title: Do not repeat the older streptomycin-first framing
sections.text: The 2025 update moved ciprofloxacin and doxycycline into first-line treatment options and added levofloxacin as first-line. Streptomycin is now a third-tier treatment option because of adverse-event concerns, limited US availability and potential administration errors associated with infrequent use. Third-tier does not mean ineffective: the source acknowledges streptomycin's efficacy. These current recommendation ranks matter more than an unqualified historical drug-of-choice mnemonic.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Changes and Updates to Previous Recommendations, numbered items 3–5.

question.stem: In a fictional board case, a nonpregnant adult with confirmed tularemia has had symptoms for 3 weeks without effective antimicrobial treatment. There is no meningitis. When comparing ciprofloxacin with doxycycline and assuming neither is contraindicated, which CDC preference is most relevant?

choices.text: Delay has no role in antimicrobial selection
A bactericidal agent such as ciprofloxacin is favored over doxycycline when treatment has been delayed more than 2 weeks
Ciprofloxacin is never recommended for tularemia
Any beta-lactam automatically replaces the tularemia regimen after 2 weeks
Doxycycline must be selected solely because it appears in the first-line list

question.explanation: The source's treatment-delay discussion favors considering a bactericidal agent, such as ciprofloxacin or gentamicin, over doxycycline after a delay greater than 2 weeks. The Box also lists ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin as preferred over doxycycline when treatment initiation is delayed.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC explicitly treats delayed effective therapy as a selection modifier.
distractorExplanations.C: Ciprofloxacin is a recommended first-line option.
distractorExplanations.D: Beta-lactams are ineffective for tularemia; delay does not make them a substitute.
distractorExplanations.E: General first-line status does not erase the specific delayed-treatment preference.

question.learningObjective: Apply the source's delayed-treatment modifier without claiming doxycycline is universally ineffective.

question.stem: A fictional adult has confirmed severe tularemia with hemodynamic instability. Effective drug options are available and no meningeal involvement is identified. Which statement best preserves both the CDC recommendation and its evidence limitation?

Severe illness never changes the initial antimicrobial approach
Only an oral beta-lactam should be considered
Consider initial aminoglycoside treatment; combination therapy may be considered, but evidence of improved severe-case outcomes is minimal
Apply an asymptomatic exposure-prophylaxis duration as the treatment plan

sources.edition: MMWR Recommendations and Reports, October 2, 2025; 74(2):1–33
sources.locator: Introduction; Recommendations: Changes and Updates, Clinical Considerations, Neuroinvasive Tularemia, prophylaxis and Pregnant Women; Box summary; Tables 1–3. Each study section has a specific sourceLocator.
sources.limitations: Treatment selection is conditional, with limited evidence for severe-disease combination benefit. Pregnancy, neonates and neuroinvasive disease have separate recommendations. No drug doses, diagnostic laboratory protocols or unrestricted antibiotic substitutions are supplied.

sections.title: Clinical forms and antibiotics that do not treat tularemia
sections.text: The guideline says ulceroglandular, pneumonic and typhoidal tularemia can be treated with the recommended ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin or doxycycline options; meningitis is a separate exception. Beta-lactams, including penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems, are ineffective for tularemia even when some laboratory susceptibility results appear favorable. Polymyxins, glycopeptides and sulfonamides are also ineffective. Do not substitute a routine beta-lactam regimen for source-supported tularemia treatment.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction — paragraph listing ineffective antimicrobial classes; Recommendations — Clinical Considerations for Treatment Recommendations, opening paragraph.

sections.title: Pregnancy-specific first-line options
sections.text: For pregnant women with tularemia, CDC recommends ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin as first-line treatment. The choice depends on severity, availability, route and side-effect considerations. Doxycycline's inclusion in the ordinary adult first-line list does not make it first-line in this pregnancy-specific list. Pregnancy postexposure prophylaxis is a different category and uses ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin as the preferred options.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — Treatment recommendation for pregnant women and Postexposure prophylaxis recommendation; Tables 2 and 3.

question.stem: A fictional adult has suspected pyogenic osteomyelitis. The probability of bone infection remains substantial, and a plain radiograph has not resolved the diagnosis. There is no MRI contraindication. Which imaging option is identified by the WikiGuidelines review as more accurate for bone-infection assessment?

choices.text: Another plain radiograph as the only test
Serial ESR as the only test
Serial CRP as the only test
MRI of the suspected site
No further evaluation because the radiograph was nondiagnostic

question.explanation: MRI is one of the more accurate imaging approaches described for osteomyelitis. A nondiagnostic plain film does not by itself settle a case with substantial ongoing suspicion.

distractorExplanations.A: Plain films can be useful for alternative diagnoses but are less accurate for this unresolved infection question.
distractorExplanations.B: The review does not find ESR sufficiently accurate to settle osteomyelitis alone.
distractorExplanations.C: The review does not find CRP sufficiently accurate to settle osteomyelitis alone.
distractorExplanations.E: A nondiagnostic plain radiograph does not eliminate substantial diagnostic suspicion.

question.learningObjective: Choose an informative imaging modality for unresolved suspected adult osteomyelitis.

sections.title: Use imaging and microbiology according to diagnostic probability
sections.text: The adult WikiGuidelines clinical review identifies MRI and certain tagged white-cell studies as more accurate imaging options for osteomyelitis than routine plain radiographs. Plain films can help when fracture or another noninfectious cause is a priority, but do not settle every suspected bone infection. Bone biopsy culture can help target antibiotics; a positive histopathology result is strongly informative, while a negative result does not reliably exclude infection.

question.stem: A fictional adult with pyogenic osteomyelitis is stable, has adequate source control and no persistent bacteremia, absorbs medication reliably and can safely follow treatment. A susceptible organism is covered by a regimen studied in osteomyelitis. Which statement best describes the antibiotic-route evidence?

choices.text: Oral therapy is a reasonable option when all selection criteria are met
Every case requires six weeks of intravenous therapy
Any oral antibiotic works regardless of susceptibility
Oral therapy requires an arbitrary minimum IV period even when criteria are met
Route selection can ignore source control

question.explanation: WikiGuidelines supports oral treatment with an appropriate studied regimen in a patient meeting the clinical, source-control, absorption and safe-use criteria. It specifies no required minimum IV lead-in once those criteria are met.

distractorExplanations.B: The source does not require IV-only treatment in every suitable adult.
distractorExplanations.C: Organism coverage and study-supported regimens are necessary; the route alone is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.D: The source does not impose a fixed minimum IV lead-in after all criteria are met.
distractorExplanations.E: Adequate source control is one of the oral-treatment criteria.

question.learningObjective: Apply oral-treatment eligibility criteria rather than equating oral therapy with undertreatment.

sections.title: Oral antibiotics can be appropriate when selection criteria are met
sections.text: WikiGuidelines gives a clear recommendation that oral therapy is a reasonable option for adult pyogenic osteomyelitis when the patient is stable, source control is adequate, bacteremia is not persistent, gastrointestinal absorption is reliable, a study-supported regimen covers likely pathogens, and circumstances permit safe use. No minimum intravenous lead-in is required once all criteria are met. This is not permission to use any oral antibiotic or overlook unstable spine disease, drainage needs or medication access.
sections.sourceLocator: Question 5: five patient-selection criteria and absence of a required minimum IV lead-in.

question.stem: A fictional adult has contiguous pyogenic osteomyelitis, no retained prosthetic implant and adequate source control. Which maximum antibiotic duration is the WikiGuidelines clear recommendation for this setting?

choices.text: Three months for all patients
Indefinite treatment
Six weeks
Two weeks for all patients
Until every image becomes normal

question.explanation: The clear recommendation is a maximum of six weeks with adequate source control and no retained implant. The guideline does not claim that exactly six weeks is necessary for every case.

distractorExplanations.A: Three months is not the stated maximum for this no-implant scenario.
distractorExplanations.B: Indefinite treatment is not the source recommendation for this adequately controlled infection.
distractorExplanations.D: A universal two-week course is not established for this setting.
distractorExplanations.E: Routine imaging normalization is not the described duration endpoint.

question.learningObjective: Keep duration recommendations tied to source control and retained-implant status.

sections.title: Duration depends on retained material and source control
sections.text: For hematogenous or contiguous adult pyogenic osteomyelitis, including diabetic-foot osteomyelitis, the source recommends a maximum six-week antibiotic course when source control is adequate and no prosthetic implant remains. It does not establish that every infection needs exactly six weeks. Shorter debrided courses and treatment after complete resection are discussed with lower certainty. A retained implant or undrained abscess falls outside this six-week recommendation.
sections.sourceLocator: Question 7: clear recommendation for osteomyelitis without a retained implant; separate clinical reviews for shorter treatment and retained implants.

sections.title: Clinical failure changes the value of repeat imaging
sections.text: The clinical review does not find that routinely repeated inflammatory markers or imaging reliably predict an individual’s long-term treatment success. Repeated imaging can be useful when treatment is clinically failing, to reconsider the diagnosis, find a drainable focus or identify a mechanical complication. Improvement should not be replaced by a rule demanding normal serial images for everyone.
sections.sourceLocator: Question 6: serial inflammatory biomarkers, routine imaging and targeted imaging in clinical failure.

question.stem: A fictional adult with possible pyogenic osteomyelitis is stable. No organism has been established, bone sampling is promptly available and there is no sepsis or threatened spinal-cord compromise. Which sequence is reasonable according to the WikiGuidelines clinical review?

choices.text: Always delay treatment for weeks regardless of progression
Select a drug only for its theoretical bone penetration
Skip microbiology because every case has the same pathogen
Use broad treatment indefinitely without seeking etiology
Obtain bone microbiology before empiric treatment if safe, while reassessing stability

question.explanation: For a stable adult with unknown etiology, obtaining bone or joint microbiology before empiric treatment can be reasonable. The review acknowledges discordant culture-yield evidence and weighs any delay against dangerous progression.

distractorExplanations.A: The review supports a conditional sampling decision, not prolonged delay despite worsening.
distractorExplanations.B: Clinical outcome evidence and patient/pathogen factors matter more than penetration theory alone.
distractorExplanations.C: Bone microbiology can identify etiology and help target treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Indefinite broad therapy ignores the source’s microbiology-guided treatment principle.

question.learningObjective: Balance microbiological diagnosis with the risk of delaying necessary treatment.

sections.title: Stable patients: balance sampling against dangerous delay
sections.text: The review considers obtaining bone or joint microbiology before starting empiric antibiotics reasonable in a clinically stable patient when the organism is not already established. This is conditional, because studies of culture-yield effects disagree. Possible sepsis, imminent spinal-cord compromise or progression of dangerous infection weighs against delay. Blood-culture identification of a likely pathogen can change the need for biopsy.
sections.sourceLocator: Questions 1 and 3: blood-culture etiology, stability, microbiological sampling and risks of delaying treatment.

sections.title: Empiric selection uses pathogen risk, not a universal drug
sections.text: In its clinical review, WikiGuidelines discusses coverage of likely gram-positive organisms and gram-negative bacilli, with MRSA and Pseudomonas coverage determined by specific risks. Local susceptibility, prior cultures, patient factors and the presence of an implant influence empiric choice; available cultures can narrow treatment. The article does not establish a single first-line antibiotic for every bone infection. Published clinical outcome evidence is more relevant than theoretical bone penetration alone.
sections.sourceLocator: Question 4: empirical selection framework, MRSA/Pseudomonas risk and bone-penetration limitations.

question.stem: A fictional adult has a high ongoing clinical suspicion of native-valve infective endocarditis despite a negative TTE. Clarifying the diagnosis will change treatment, and transesophageal imaging is feasible. Which next study is most supported by the diagnostic review?

choices.text: Another negative TTE automatically settles the diagnosis
No imaging because cultures alone always establish valve involvement
Transesophageal echocardiography
A plain chest radiograph to exclude endocarditis
Serial CRP alone to establish an infected valve

question.explanation: TEE is more sensitive than TTE and is useful when substantial unacceptable diagnostic probability remains after a negative TTE and the result will change treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: The impact of a negative TTE depends on probability and image quality.
distractorExplanations.B: Blood cultures provide microbiology but do not replace the imaging assessment in this vignette.
distractorExplanations.D: A plain chest film is not the source’s next valve-focused imaging option.
distractorExplanations.E: CRP alone does not establish valve infection in the described diagnostic framework.

question.learningObjective: Use pretest probability when interpreting a negative TTE in suspected endocarditis.

sections.title: Diagnosis integrates clinical, microbiological and imaging findings
sections.text: The WikiGuidelines diagnostic review describes Duke-based schemas, including the 2023 Duke-ISCVID update, as practical tools incorporating clinical, microbiological and imaging criteria. Pathology is the reference standard but often is not available during initial treatment decisions. This abbreviated module does not reproduce a complete diagnostic score or claim that an isolated symptom establishes infective endocarditis.
sections.sourceLocator: Part 1 Question 1: pathology, Duke-based schemas and diagnostic information types.

sections.title: A negative transthoracic study must be interpreted with probability
sections.text: TEE is more sensitive than TTE for adult infective endocarditis. The diagnostic review considers TEE useful when an unacceptably high probability remains after a negative TTE and clarification will change treatment; it is also useful for prosthetic-valve evaluation and suspected complications such as perivalvular abscess. A negative TTE can be reassuring in selected low-probability circumstances, not every high-suspicion case.
sections.sourceLocator: Part 1 Question 6: pretest probability, TTE quality and reasons to obtain TEE.

question.stem: A fictional adult is stable with suspected infective endocarditis. Antibiotics have not started and blood sampling can be obtained promptly. Which sequence best preserves etiologic information according to the source?

choices.text: Begin antibiotics, then intentionally wait days before sampling
Obtain appropriate blood-culture sets before antibiotics when feasible
Use only a urine culture to identify the valve pathogen
Omit microbiology if a murmur is present
Collect cultures only after the antibiotic course is complete

question.explanation: When feasible, blood cultures should precede antibiotics because prior exposure lowers recovery of the causative organism. This stable vignette does not justify a rule to delay treatment in an unstable patient.

distractorExplanations.A: Antibiotic exposure can reduce blood-culture yield.
distractorExplanations.C: Urine culture does not replace blood cultures for this suspected endovascular infection.
distractorExplanations.D: The diagnostic framework needs microbiological information; a murmur alone is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.E: Waiting until treatment completion sacrifices the opportunity to establish etiology early.

question.learningObjective: Protect blood-culture yield without turning sampling into a reason for dangerous treatment delay.

sections.title: When feasible, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics
sections.text: In suspected adult infective endocarditis, obtaining blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible improves the chance of recovering the organism. The review discusses several properly filled culture sets rather than a single bottle. Previous antibiotic exposure can lower yield. This principle does not authorize delaying urgent treatment in an unstable patient and does not establish a complete culture-negative-endocarditis algorithm.

question.stem: A fictional adult receiving IV treatment for bacterial endocarditis is stable. Bacteremia is clearing, no immediate cardiac procedure is needed, gastrointestinal absorption is reliable and a studied oral regimen covers the susceptible organism. Safe medication access and follow-up are established. Which option best matches WikiGuidelines?

choices.text: Consider transition to the supported oral regimen after the selection review
Switch to any available oral antibiotic regardless of susceptibility
Require IV-only treatment in every suitable case
Stop all antibiotics because bacteremia is clearing
Ignore cardiac source control once oral medication is available

question.explanation: Appropriate oral transitional treatment is a reasonable option for selected adults. The drug, organism, clinical course, source-control needs, absorption and practical safety all matter.

distractorExplanations.B: Oral treatment still requires a susceptible organism and a regimen supported by clinical data.
distractorExplanations.C: The source’s clear recommendation supports oral transition as an option in suitable adults.
distractorExplanations.D: Clearing bacteremia does not establish that the treatment course is complete.
distractorExplanations.E: Immediate surgical and source-control needs remain part of selection.

question.learningObjective: Recognize selected adult endocarditis patients in whom appropriate oral transition can be considered.

sections.title: Oral transition is an option for selected adults, not any regimen
sections.text: WikiGuidelines gives a clear recommendation that transition from initial intravenous to appropriate oral treatment can be a reasonable option in adult bacterial infective endocarditis. Its patient-selection clinical review considers stability, no immediate surgical or procedural source-control need, clearing or cleared bacteremia, a susceptible organism, a published-data-supported oral regimen, reliable absorption and circumstances allowing safe therapy. The required IV lead-in duration and optimal regimen are not established as universal rules.
sections.sourceLocator: Part 4 Questions 3 and 4: trial-supported oral transition, clinical selection criteria and uncertain IV lead-in.

question.stem: A fictional adult with infective endocarditis has prosthetic cardiac material and a perivalvular abscess. Which organizational approach best reflects the WikiGuidelines clinical review for complex disease?

choices.text: Treat every case within one specialty regardless of complications
Transfer every patient automatically because randomized trials prove a universal rule
Use microbiology alone without cardiac assessment
Coordinate infectious disease, pharmacy, cardiology and cardiac surgery expertise
Use an antibiotic-route decision to eliminate procedural assessment

question.explanation: The review describes a multidisciplinary team for complex endocarditis, with infectious disease, pharmacy, cardiology and cardiac surgery among the core disciplines. Evidence for team benefit is observational; a universal transfer rule is not established.

distractorExplanations.A: Prosthetic material and an abscess are complex features for coordinated expertise.
distractorExplanations.B: The source reports no randomized evidence establishing a universal transfer rule.
distractorExplanations.C: Microbiology alone does not cover the cardiac and procedural complications in this case.
distractorExplanations.E: Changing medication route does not address the abscess or remove assessment for intervention.

question.learningObjective: Coordinate specialist expertise for endocarditis complicated by prosthetic material and abscess.

sections.title: Complex disease benefits from access to several disciplines
sections.text: The WikiGuidelines clinical review describes multidisciplinary endocarditis teams involving infectious disease, pharmacy, cardiology and cardiac surgery, with other specialists according to complications and availability. Observational studies suggest benefit, but no randomized trials establish a universal team-transfer rule. Hemodynamic instability, heart failure, prosthetic material, abscesses and embolic complications are examples of complex circumstances needing coordinated expertise.

question.stem: A fictional adult with newly evaluated metastatic breast cancer is being discussed in an ASCO resource-constrained setting. Reliable pathology and biomarker testing are available. Which information should guide treatment selection rather than using the same regimen for every tumor?

choices.text: The patient’s age alone
Menopausal status plus pathological and hormone-receptor/HER2 features
Medication price alone, regardless of tumor biology
The primary-tumor side alone
Whether symptoms have been present for an arbitrary number of weeks

question.explanation: ASCO recommends using reliable pathological and biomarker features, and menopausal status affects endocrine choices. The article concerns resource-constrained metastatic care rather than a universal Maximal-setting protocol.

distractorExplanations.A: Age alone does not replace menopausal and tumor-biological assessment.
distractorExplanations.C: Resources matter but do not justify ignoring reliable tumor biology.
distractorExplanations.D: Tumor side alone does not supply the biological selection framework.
distractorExplanations.E: An arbitrary symptom duration does not replace the described assessment.

question.learningObjective: Use tumor biology and menopausal status to frame metastatic-breast treatment selection.

sections.text: The ASCO resource-stratified guideline concerns adults with metastatic breast cancer in resource-constrained settings, not a complete Maximal-resource protocol. question.stem: In a fictional study case in an ASCO resource-constrained setting, a premenopausal patient with hormone-receptor-positive disease is being considered for an aromatase inhibitor. Which accompanying intervention is required by the source’s eligibility principle?

choices.text: No accompanying ovarian intervention
Empiric antibiotics
Routine radiation to every metastatic site
Ovarian suppression or ablation
Stopping all symptom-support measures

question.explanation: The guideline states that premenopausal patients receive aromatase inhibitors only with ovarian suppression or ablation. This principle does not establish the full regimen or drug sequence for every setting.

distractorExplanations.A: An aromatase inhibitor alone does not meet the stated premenopausal condition.
distractorExplanations.B: Antibiotics do not supply the ovarian intervention in the source.
distractorExplanations.C: Radiation to every metastatic site is not the required accompanying endocrine intervention.
distractorExplanations.E: Symptom support is not replaced by endocrine-treatment selection.

question.learningObjective: Recognize the ovarian-function boundary for aromatase inhibition in premenopausal disease.

At presentation, alongside the other care assessments

sections.text: ASCO’s resource-stratified metastatic-breast guideline calls for identifying and addressing palliative-care needs at presentation for all patients, including when antineoplastic treatment is unavailable. question.stem: A fictional postmenopausal adult has hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer without life-threatening or highly symptomatic disease. choices.text: Hormonal therapy alone when otherwise appropriate
No treatment solely because the combination is unavailable
An HER2-targeted regimen selected regardless of HER2 status
Combination chemotherapy as a mandatory substitute for every patient
A regimen chosen without pathology or receptor information

question.explanation: For the resource-constrained setting addressed, ASCO preserves hormonal monotherapy when the AI/CDK4/6 combination is unavailable. The question excludes the severity qualifications that change the choice and does not define the best complete US high-resource regimen.

sections.title: Match metastatic treatment to biology, menopause and resources
sections.text: The ASCO resource-stratified guideline concerns adults with metastatic breast cancer in resource-constrained settings, not a complete Maximal-resource protocol. It advises treatment according to pathological and biomarker features when reliable testing is available, including hormone-receptor and HER2 status, and emphasizes menopausal assessment. Cases should be discussed with a multidisciplinary team. Resource-constrained alternatives must not be presented as a universally preferred United States regimen.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction; General Notes 3 and 4; First-Line — Hormone Receptor-Positive.

sections.title: When a recommended combination is unavailable, preserve an endocrine option
sections.text: For hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic disease in the resource-constrained settings addressed, ASCO recommends hormonal therapy alone when the nonsteroidal aromatase-inhibitor/CDK4/6-inhibitor combination is unavailable. Life-threatening or highly symptomatic disease has different considerations; the guideline discusses chemotherapy in that context. An availability-based alternative should not be mislabeled the universally best high-resource first-line regimen.

question.stem: A 27-year-old nonsmoker with confirmed migraine with aura requests an estrogen-containing combined pill. No other stroke risk factors are identified. Which counseling statement matches U.S. MEC?

The pill is category 2 because she does not smoke
The pill is category 4; discuss acceptable alternative methods
The pill is category 3 only during an active headache
Every contraceptive method is category 4 for migraine aura

question.explanation: Migraine with aura is category 4 for combined hormonal contraception. This classification is method-specific, so counseling should consider alternatives and preferences.

question.stem: A patient requests a copper IUD. No CDC history criterion establishes that she is not pregnant, and the urine pregnancy test is negative. Which next step follows U.S. SPR?

choices.text: Insert the IUD because a negative urine test is always definitive
Offer an appropriate non-IUD method until pregnancy can reasonably be excluded
Insert the IUD if she signs a statement accepting uncertainty
Repeat the same urine test immediately and disregard the history
Avoid offering any contraceptive method until the next annual visit

question.explanation: A negative test alone does not establish certainty when none of the CDC history criteria is met. CDC recommends a method other than an IUD until certainty is established.

distractorExplanations.A: The source explicitly describes this test limitation.
distractorExplanations.C: Consent does not establish pregnancy certainty.
distractorExplanations.D: An immediate repeat does not remove the stated history limitation.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC provides an interim contraceptive option rather than an annual delay.

question.learningObjective: Distinguish pregnancy-test negativity from reasonable pregnancy exclusion before IUD placement.

Wait at least 5 days, then restart; use barriers or abstain for 7 days after restarting or until next menses, whichever comes first
Wait 24 hours, then restart without backup
Restart today and use barriers for exactly 24 hours
Wait 30 days before every hormonal method, including provider-administered methods

sections.text: For a community-dwelling older adult found to be at fall risk, CDC STEADI proceeds to assessment of modifiable contributors and fall history. Preserve the dose without reviewing its indication or alternatives
Choose eye-care referral as the only intervention despite a medication contributor
Stop every medicine abruptly without individual assessment

sections.title: Sudden visual warning pattern
sections.text: Retinal detachment separates the retina from its usual position. A sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, or a dark curtain or shadow across vision is a warning pattern. A small detachment can be asymptomatic; absence of the full pattern does not exclude it.

sections.title: Emergency recognition
sections.text: NEI describes retinal detachment as a medical emergency. A hypothetical learner should choose immediate eye-doctor or emergency-department evaluation for its warning symptoms, because delay can allow more retina to detach and increase the risk of permanent vision loss.
sections.sourceLocator: Symptoms, emergency and delayed-treatment paragraphs; At a glance urgent warning.

question.stem: A dilated examination raises concern for retinal detachment, but the eye doctor still needs to define the position of the retina. Which additional assessment most directly matches that remaining question in the NEI reference?

choices.text: Visual-acuity testing to measure clarity
Ocular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography to show retinal position
Visual-field testing to assess peripheral vision
Tonometry to measure eye pressure
Eye-muscle testing to assess movement

question.explanation: NEI describes ocular ultrasound or OCT when additional information about retinal position is needed after dilation. The other tests measure different aspects of eye function.

distractorExplanations.A: Visual acuity measures clarity rather than the retinal position asked about.
distractorExplanations.C: Visual-field testing evaluates side vision rather than the retinal position asked about.
distractorExplanations.D: Tonometry measures pressure rather than retinal position.
distractorExplanations.E: Eye-muscle testing assesses muscle function rather than retinal position.

question.learningObjective: Choose additional eye assessment according to the unresolved clinical question.

sections.title: Retinal examination and additional imaging
sections.text: A dilated eye examination is used to inspect the retina for a tear or detachment. If the eye doctor needs more information after that examination, ocular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography can help show retinal position. The reference does not establish a substitute home assessment or a numerical test-accuracy claim. In NEI's examination overview, visual acuity checks clarity, a visual-field test checks side vision, eye-muscle testing checks muscle function and tonometry measures pressure. These test purposes differ from imaging the retinal position.

question.stem: A specialist identifies a small retinal tear and considers a procedure intended to seal that tear. Which procedure and purpose match the NEI reference?

Laser treatment or cryopexy to seal the retinal break
Surgical repositioning of a larger detached retinal area

sections.title: Treatment depends on extent and type
sections.text: Small retinal holes or tears may be sealed with laser treatment or cryopexy. A larger detachment may require surgery to return the retina to position. The choice depends on extent and detachment type; this reference does not support selecting a particular operative method for every case. Other NEI references describe glaucoma drops and drainage-directed laser treatment for eye pressure, and cataract surgery to replace a clouded lens. These target different problems from sealing a retinal tear.

sections.title: Recognize an acute angle-closure pattern
sections.text: Sudden intense eye pain with a red eye, blurred vision and nausea is the acute angle-closure warning pattern described by NEI. It requires immediate medical evaluation. Symptoms support concern in a hypothetical case but do not establish a confirmed diagnosis without examination.
sections.sourceLocator: Types of Glaucoma: Angle-closure glaucoma, emergency warning and symptom list.

sections.title: Blocked drainage and rapid pressure rise
sections.text: In angle-closure glaucoma the outer edge of the iris obstructs fluid drainage from the front of the eye. Fluid accumulation can rapidly raise eye pressure. Untreated acute disease can cause blindness within days; the clinical teaching priority is urgent evaluation, not a home waiting period. NEI distinguishes other glaucoma mechanisms: new vessels can cover drainage structures in neovascular glaucoma; shed iris pigment can obstruct drainage in pigmentary glaucoma; deposited material can obstruct drainage in exfoliation glaucoma; inflammation or scarring may impair drainage in uveitic glaucoma. These are distinct from the acute iris-edge blockage described here.
sections.sourceLocator: Types of Glaucoma: Angle-closure glaucoma, mechanism and untreated-course paragraph.; Secondary glaucomas: Neovascular, Pigmentary, Exfoliation and Uveitic glaucoma mechanism paragraphs.

sections.title: Acute and chronic angle closure differ
sections.text: The same NEI reference also describes slow or chronic angle-closure glaucoma, which develops more gradually and may be asymptomatic. Do not transfer the slow course to a vignette with sudden painful visual symptoms or assume all angle closure has the same presentation.
sections.sourceLocator: Types of Glaucoma: Angle-closure glaucoma, final slow/chronic paragraph.

question.stem: A specialist confirms acute angle-closure glaucoma with rapidly rising eye pressure. Which drainage-blocking mechanism matches that diagnosis in the NEI subtype descriptions?

Extra deposited material obstructing fluid drainage
The outer edge of the iris blocking front-of-eye drainage
Inflammation or scarring impairing fluid drainage

question.explanation: NEI attributes acute angle closure to the outer iris edge blocking drainage. Its other subtype descriptions associate the alternative mechanisms with neovascular, pigmentary, exfoliation or uveitic glaucoma.

distractorExplanations.A: NEI describes this mechanism in neovascular glaucoma rather than acute angle closure.
distractorExplanations.B: NEI describes shed iris pigment in pigmentary glaucoma.
distractorExplanations.C: NEI describes extra deposited material in exfoliation glaucoma.
distractorExplanations.E: NEI describes possible inflammatory or scarring effects in uveitic glaucoma.

question.learningObjective: Distinguish acute angle-closure drainage obstruction from other sourced glaucoma mechanisms.

sections.title: Lens clouding and visual symptoms
sections.text: A cataract is clouding of the eye lens. Early cataracts may cause no symptoms; progression can produce cloudy or blurred vision, faded colors, glare or halos and trouble seeing at night. These symptoms can also occur with other eye problems and warrant eye assessment. The confirmed clouded lens differs from retinal detachment, where the retina separates from its usual position, and glaucoma, which damages the optic nerve. Open-angle, normal-tension and acute angle-closure glaucoma have their separate NEI descriptions; lens clouding alone does not establish those diagnoses. NEI identifies normal-tension glaucoma as an open-angle subtype at normal eye pressure and acute angle closure as iris-edge blockage of drainage.

sections.title: Stage IV identifies metastatic colon cancer — source excerpt
sections.text: Stage IV colon cancer is also called metastatic colon cancer. Metastatic cancer happens when cancer cells travel through the lymphatic system or blood and form tumors in other parts of the body. The metastatic tumor is the same type of cancer as the primary tumor. For example, if colon cancer spreads to the liver, the cancer cells in the liver are actually colon cancer cells. The disease is called metastatic colon cancer, not liver cancer. Learn more in Metastatic Cancer: When Cancer Spreads.

question.stem: A hypothetical patient with clinically localized prostate cancer chooses to defer treatment while attending regular follow-up, with local therapy planned with curative intent if the tumor progresses. Which strategy best matches the cited NCI distinction?

sections.title: Watchful waiting follows a palliative-intent strategy — source excerpt
sections.text: Watchful waiting and active surveillance/active monitoring are the most commonly used terms, and the literature does not always clearly distinguish them, making the interpretation of results difficult. The general concept of watchful waiting is patient follow-up with the application of palliative care as needed to alleviate symptoms of tumor progression. There is no planned attempt at curative therapy at any point in follow-up.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment Option Overview > Watchful Waiting or Active Surveillance/Active Monitoring; complete distinction paragraph.

sections.title: Active surveillance preserves later curative-intent treatment — source excerpt
sections.text:
In contrast, the strategy behind active surveillance/active monitoring is to defer therapy for clinically localized disease but regularly follow the patient and initiate local therapy with curative intent if there are any signs of local tumor progression.[6-9] The intention is to avoid the morbidity of therapy in men who have indolent or nonprogressive disease but preserve the ability to cure them should the tumor progress. Active surveillance/active monitoring often involves:

• Regular patient visits.
• Digital rectal examinations.
• Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing.
• Transrectal ultrasound (in some series).
• Transrectal needle biopsies (in some series).
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment Option Overview > Watchful Waiting or Active Surveillance/Active Monitoring; complete intent paragraph and often-involves list, references 6–9. No surveillance intervals or intervention thresholds are imported.

sections.title: Localized treatment selection includes patient context — source excerpt
sections.text: In younger patients (aged 50–60 years) whose expected survival is long, treatment should be considered.[3] Radical prostatectomy, external-beam radiation therapy (EBRT), interstitial implantation of radioisotopes, and watchful waiting and active surveillance/active monitoring yield apparently similar survival rates in noncontrolled, selected series. The decision to treat should be made in the context of the patient’s age, associated medical illnesses, and personal desires.[3]
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment of Stage I Prostate Cancer > Overview; complete treatment-selection paragraph, reference 3. Apparent similarity is from noncontrolled selected series, not a guarantee or proof of equivalence.

sections.title: Observation can be considered for selected older or ill patients — source excerpt
sections.text: Asymptomatic patients of advanced age or with concomitant illness may warrant careful observation without immediate active treatment.[3,4] Watch and wait, observation, expectant management, and active surveillance/active monitoring are terms indicating a strategy that does not employ immediate therapy with curative intent.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment Option Overview for Prostate Cancer > Watchful Waiting or Active Surveillance/Active Monitoring; opening paragraph and references 3–4. May warrant, asymptomatic and concomitant-illness qualifiers are retained.

sections.title: Watchful waiting follows a palliative-intent strategy — source excerpt
sections.text: Watchful waiting and active surveillance/active monitoring are the most commonly used terms, and the literature does not always clearly distinguish them, making the interpretation of results difficult. The general concept of watchful waiting is patient follow-up with the application of palliative care as needed to alleviate symptoms of tumor progression. There is no planned attempt at curative therapy at any point in follow-up.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment Option Overview > Watchful Waiting or Active Surveillance/Active Monitoring; complete distinction paragraph.

sections.title: Active surveillance preserves later curative-intent treatment — source excerpt
sections.text:
In contrast, the strategy behind active surveillance/active monitoring is to defer therapy for clinically localized disease but regularly follow the patient and initiate local therapy with curative intent if there are any signs of local tumor progression.[6-9] The intention is to avoid the morbidity of therapy in men who have indolent or nonprogressive disease but preserve the ability to cure them should the tumor progress. Active surveillance/active monitoring often involves:

• Regular patient visits.
• Digital rectal examinations.
• Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing.
• Transrectal ultrasound (in some series).
• Transrectal needle biopsies (in some series).
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment Option Overview > Watchful Waiting or Active Surveillance/Active Monitoring; complete intent paragraph and often-involves list, references 6–9. No surveillance intervals or intervention thresholds are imported.

sources.locator: What Are Health Literacy Universal Precautions?; Why Use Health Literacy Universal Precautions?

sections.title: Use universal precautions
sections.text: Difficulty understanding health information cannot reliably be inferred from appearance or education. AHRQ recommends making communication understandable and confirming comprehension with everyone.

question.stem: In a fictional teaching encounter, an explanation has been given using familiar language. Which question best checks understanding?

choices.text: How would you describe the main steps in your own words?
You understand everything, correct?
Could you repeat each technical term exactly?
Can we assume the handout answered everything?
Would you agree that the explanation was simple?

question.explanation: Asking for an explanation in the person’s own words helps confirm understanding of the important information.

distractorExplanations.B: A yes-or-no response provides limited evidence.
distractorExplanations.C: Repeating terms does not demonstrate the main meaning.
distractorExplanations.D: A handout alone does not confirm comprehension.
distractorExplanations.E: Perceived simplicity does not demonstrate understanding.

question.learningObjective: Distinguish an open comprehension check from reassurance-seeking questions.

sources.title: Communicate Clearly: Tool 4
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed April 2024
sources.locator: Actions: clear spoken communication and confirming understanding

sections.title: Plain language
sections.text: Use familiar words, a clear pace and a limited set of important points. Replace jargon and vague descriptions with concrete explanations.

sections.title: Confirm understanding
sections.text: Ask the person to explain important information in their own words. This gives more information about understanding than a yes-or-no question about whether everything is clear.

question.stem: In a fictional improvement exercise, a team wants to test a new reminder. Which initial plan best follows the PDSA method?

choices.text: Deploy everywhere without defining an outcome
Decide success only from enthusiasm
Avoid observing workflow during the test
Promise the first design will never change
Test a small change, define a measure and time frame, then review results

question.explanation: A small, measurable test supports learning before adaptation or broader implementation.

distractorExplanations.A: This removes the opportunity for a defined small test.
distractorExplanations.B: Enthusiasm alone does not assess the planned result.
distractorExplanations.C: Observations inform learning during the test.
distractorExplanations.D: Iteration is part of the method.

question.learningObjective: Identify a small, measurable improvement test in an exam scenario.

sources.title: Plan-Do-Study-Act Worksheet, Directions, and Examples
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed March 2024
sources.locator: PDSA directions; Plan, Do, Study and Act

sections.title: Test and learn
sections.text: PDSA plans a small change and a measurement, tries it, studies the results, then adapts or expands based on learning. Small, brief tests can precede broader implementation.

question.stem: In a fictional safety vignette, several staff members have nearly selected the wrong item from the same confusing electronic menu. Which response best addresses recurrence from a systems perspective?

choices.text: Label only the latest staff member as careless
Declare safety assured because no harm occurred
Investigate the interface and workflow, redesign contributing hazards and evaluate the change
Require everyone to memorize the current menu permanently
Suppress reports to improve the safety statistics

question.explanation: A recurring interface hazard calls for investigation of contributing system factors and evaluation of corrective changes.

distractorExplanations.A: Individual blame alone leaves the recurring hazard.
distractorExplanations.B: A near miss can reveal a vulnerability.
distractorExplanations.D: Memorization alone leaves the confusing design.
distractorExplanations.E: Suppressing reports hides opportunities for prevention.

question.learningObjective: Identify a systems response to a recurring fictional safety hazard.

sources.title: System-Focused Event Investigation and Analysis Guide
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: CANDOR Toolkit; page last reviewed August 2022
sources.locator: A Systems Approach; follow-up and measurement

sections.title: Identify system factors
sections.text: Safety-event investigation examines contributing processes, technology and working conditions. Its prevention goal requires addressing system vulnerabilities and measuring whether changes work.

topic.name: Social needs, equity and resource connections

question.stem: In a fictional exam scenario, two people live in the same neighborhood. One cannot afford food while the other has stable food access. Which statement best distinguishes social determinants from individual social needs?

choices.text: Neighborhood residence makes their individual needs identical
Shared community conditions can coexist with different individual social needs
Food insecurity is unrelated to social context
A person’s social needs are determined solely by diagnosis
Community information replaces asking about individual circumstances

question.explanation: AHRQ distinguishes community-level conditions from individuals’ differing social needs within that community.

distractorExplanations.A: Shared location does not make needs identical.
distractorExplanations.C: Food insecurity is a listed social need.
distractorExplanations.D: Diagnosis alone does not describe social needs.
distractorExplanations.E: Individual circumstances still matter.

question.learningObjective: Distinguish shared community conditions from differing individual social needs.

sources.title: About SDOH in Healthcare
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Page last reviewed February 2020
sources.locator: SDOH in Communities; Social Needs

sections.title: Community context and individual needs
sections.text: Community conditions include transportation, food availability and access to services. People in the same community can have different individual social needs, such as food insecurity or financial strain.

topic.name: Social needs, equity and resource connections

question.stem: In a fictional exam encounter, a person requests transportation help and agrees to a resource referral. Which next action best completes the support process?

choices.text: Give an old number and assume access succeeded
Contact every relative without permission
Record the referral and never check its result
Confirm the resource connection and address barriers if it was not completed
Treat a positive social-needs screen as refusal of all care

question.explanation: AHRQ recommends following up to learn whether a referral was completed and documenting its outcome.

distractorExplanations.A: An unverified connection may leave the need unmet.
distractorExplanations.B: Sharing requires the person’s permission.
distractorExplanations.C: Referral placement alone does not establish completion.
distractorExplanations.E: A social need is not a refusal of care.

question.learningObjective: Recognize follow-through after a requested fictional resource referral.

sources.title: Attend to Social Needs: Tool 18
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed April 2024
sources.locator: Assess social needs and support systems; connect with resources; follow up

sections.title: Ask respectfully
sections.text: Explain why social questions are being asked and how information will be used. Discuss needs privately, ask what help is wanted and obtain permission before sharing with support contacts.

sections.title: Close the referral loop
sections.text: Support connections to appropriate community resources, help with access barriers and follow up to determine whether a requested referral was completed. Keep resource information current.
